description: I’m Aashi, a CSE student who loves space, building things and telling stories with data. I’m part of a space club and a robotics club. I want to turn NASA data into a story people feel, not just read. Looking for a writer, a designer or illustrator, and someone who can edit video or animate. No experience needed, just curiosity and the will to finish what we start.
summary:
Not Forgotten is an interactive web story about 22 machines NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space, from Surveyor 3 in 1967 to the ten sample tubes Perseverance set down at Three Forks in 2023. Most accounts of abandoned hardware are inventories. NASA's 2012 lunar catalogue alone lists 796 items. A list tells you what is out there, but not how each machine stopped or why it still matters.

We tell every machine the same way: its last words, the cause of its silence, and what it passed on. Each ending is sorted into eight causes, from design limits and harsh environments to human error, and every claim is labelled by how certain the record is, so a probable cause is never presented as proven. An inheritance map traces 19 links between machines and separates reused hardware from design heritage and from knowledge.

Visitors can take a 90-second guided journey, turn 3D models of Earth, the Moon and Mars, watch a live silence clock, or use the quiz and classroom activities. The story ends on a question: when we send something into the unknown, how much responsibility do we have for what remains?
details:
Not Forgotten is a scroll-driven website that travels outward from Earth to the Moon, Mars and deep space, stopping at 22 NASA machines that were left behind, lost, switched off, or are still travelling. Each machine opens into a ledger with three parts. The Last Words gives its final transmission, or for craft still working, its latest verified milestone. The Cause of Silence places its ending in one or more of eight categories: design limit, human decision, environment, engineering, human error, distance and power, unresolved, and still active. The Inheritance shows what it handed to later missions.

The archive below the journey reorganises the same 22 machines in different ways. A cause board groups them by why they went quiet. An inheritance map draws 19 links between them, each marked as reused hardware, design heritage or knowledge, so an influence is never presented as reused parts. One link runs backwards in time: Phoenix's 2008 discovery of perchlorate changed how scientists read Viking's 1976 soil results. A silence clock counts the time since each machine was last heard and shows whether people chose to stop it. A time machine, an "overachievers" comparison of designed and actual lifespans, a mission control view, a quiz and a six-activity classroom pack give visitors other ways in. A 90-second guided journey with pause, skip and exit controls introduces four machines for anyone short on time. The site closes with what we choose to leave behind: the One Small Step to Protect Human Heritage in Space Act, the Three Forks sample depot waiting for a mission that has not been funded, and the question of what responsibility we carry for what remains.

Every fact was checked against NASA mission pages, NASA History Office and JPL records, NASA technical reports and investigation documents, with reputable reporting used only where those are silent. Each claim carries a label: verified, historical record, most probable explanation, unresolved, or estimated. Mars Polar Lander's cause is shown as the most probable explanation, not proven fact. Reports of ALSEP signals after the September 30, 1977 shutdown are shown as disputed. The Voyagers are listed as still active, with switched-off instruments kept separate from lost contact. Every photograph is a credited NASA image.

The project turns a list of objects into stories a student, teacher or general reader can follow in minutes and explore for longer. It shows that space exploration is built on earlier machines, including failed ones, and it asks readers to think about responsibility for what we leave on other worlds. The classroom pack and quiz let teachers use it directly.

Three.js for the 3D scenes, GSAP ScrollTrigger for scroll animation, Vite with vite-plugin-singlefile to build a single self-contained page, and plain JavaScript, HTML and CSS. Hosted on Netlify. Photographs load from the NASA Image and Video Library. Planet surfaces use Solar System Scope textures (CC BY 4.0), and Earth's night lights use NASA's Black Marble imagery. No login, no tracking, and it works on phones.

We avoided presenting any disputed or probable cause as settled, and kept deliberate scientific assets such as the sample depot separate from failed equipment. We followed the rule against NASA logos and insignia. We designed for accessibility: keyboard navigation, alt text on every photo, reduced-motion support, and no autoplaying sound.
